1

Your request — the mega menu

“Yes, I want a mega menu. What you are seeing now is a lot of subcategories and filters.” — with a Mega Menu Layout.docx attached describing the intended structure.

We reviewed the attached structure in full. It is buildable, and we can deliver it in 12 hours for desktop and mobile. There is one structural change to agree first.

1.1 One thing to resolve first — depth

Blocker to confirm before build: the structure in Mega Menu Layout.docx goes five levels deep (Brand → Machine → Part-specific option → Level 4 → Level 5). Shopify’s navigation supports a maximum of three levels. The structure has to be condensed to three levels before it can be built.

What we recommend. Condense the structure to three levels. In practice that means keeping the three tiers customers actually navigate by, and merging the deeper tiers upward into level 3:

  • Level 1 — top-level entry (e.g. Shop, or a brand).
  • Level 2 — product group (e.g. Paint & Refinishing, Prep & Masking).
  • Level 3 — the category the customer lands on (e.g. Masking Tape). Anything currently sitting below this — Fine Line, Foam, Attachment, Standard Masking Tape — is either promoted to sit alongside it at level 3, or left out of the navigation.

You know the catalogue far better than we do, so the merge decisions are best made on your side. Please send us the revised three-level structure — or tell us which tiers you want merged and we will draft it for your approval. Either way, this needs to be agreed before the build starts.

1.2 Layout

The structure currently resolves to six columns. Two consequences:

  • Six columns on one row needs a full-width mega menu panel — that is the better-looking option.
  • Constrained inside the site container, six columns will wrap onto two rows.

We recommend the full-width panel.

A richer variant combines the multi-column category links with promotional banners on the right — worth considering for seasonal offers and brand pushes:

1.3 Effort

Mega menu, full-width, three-level, desktop and mobile: 12 hours — $420. Full costing in Section 5.

Our honest recommendation, before you decide. The mega menu on its own is a real improvement, but it is a new front door on a storefront that has bigger problems behind it. Section 2 sets out what we found while reviewing the site — please read it before choosing between the two options.
2

Beyond the menu — what we’d redesign and rebuild

While reviewing both the live site and the target Shopify Plus store, our design lead ran a full UI/UX audit of the current storefront. Genesis Auto Body Supply has a large catalogue — hundreds of SKUs across paints, primers, clearcoats, abrasives, masking, tools and equipment. For a catalogue this size, UI/UX is not decoration: it is the mechanism that gets a customer from landing page to the right product. That mechanism is currently underperforming.

You are paying for Shopify Plus, but the current front end is still built like a traditional catalogue site — heavy on images, thin on product discovery, and weak on mobile. Everything below is what we would change, and it is what Option B covers.

Cross-cutting issue — text baked into images. Large parts of the homepage are image tiles with the product name, price and offer rendered inside the image. Search engines cannot read that text, so none of it contributes to SEO, and it cannot be re-used or translated. Anything promotional should be real HTML text over a real image.

2.1 Header & navigation

The header does not yet carry a brand direction. The navigation bar uses a blue that appears nowhere else in the design system, so it reads as a bolted-on component rather than the start of the brand identity.

Recommendation: promote the navigation blue to the site’s primary brand colour and carry it through buttons, links, section headings and the footer. The header then stops being just navigation and becomes the anchor of a strong, professional, technical-trade brand identity.

The dropdowns are the second problem. A dropdown holding two links wastes the pattern entirely:

Conversely, with this many product lines, the top-level categories deserve their own dedicated entry point — either the mega menu from Section 1, or a vertical “Shop All Categories” panel alongside it:

2.2 Homepage

Two distinct problems.

The promo tile grid is visually noisy. A four-row grid of near-identical bordered tiles gives the eye nowhere to rest. If this merchandising block stays, it should be a single row.

Banners run back-to-back with no breathing room. The homepage stacks banner after banner, which makes it feel like a printed catalogue or a flyer rather than an eCommerce storefront designed to lead a customer somewhere.

  • Banners sit flush against each other with no whitespace — the page is visually heavy.
  • The banners share a near-identical design treatment but carry different messages, so the page reads as repetitive and monotonous instead of establishing a hierarchy.

The homepage needs a visual rhythm and a deliberate flow. Our proposed section order:

Hero → Popular Categories → Best Sellers / On Sale → Brand Trust → Banner → Products → The Support (important for a technical trade audience) → Products

Product cards should also gain Add to cart and Quick view, so customers can buy from a listing without loading a product page — significant for repeat trade buyers restocking known SKUs.

2.3 Footer

2.4 Collection pages

This is where a catalogue this large wins or loses the sale, and where the current site is weakest.

  • Add the filters that actually matter in this industry: price, brand, size, grit, VOC, mix ratio, and similar technical attributes. This is the single highest-impact change on the page.
  • Remove the List/Condensed/Grid view switcher. It adds clutter and is rarely used when shopping.
  • Use pagination rather than infinite “load more” — with this many products, pagination gives customers a sense of position and lets them return to where they were.

The sidebar filter itself needs rework — it is currently raw and unstyled:

  • Give the sidebar a light background so it reads as a distinct panel.
  • Truncate long filter groups to roughly 10 entries with a Show more toggle that reveals the rest on click.

2.5 Product pages

Recommendations: surface purchase benefits (warranty, returns, free shipping, tech support) directly on the page, and display the support phone number prominently — trade buyers call before they buy. Then add cross-sell:

2.6 Mobile / responsive

The current site does not meet the responsive standard modern shoppers expect. On mobile the layout is cramped, the navigation collapses to a bare hamburger, and search, filtering and add-to-cart are all awkward.

Customers now arrive across a wide range of screen sizes and expect a layout that is responsive, readable and easy to operate — particularly for search, filtering, browsing products and adding to cart. Mobile needs to be a first-class target in this project, not an afterthought.

2.7 Summary

The current interface still carries the characteristics of a traditional catalogue website: navigation and categories are not intuitive, several areas depend on images instead of real content, product discovery is not optimised, and the overall experience is not continuous from arrival to purchase.

The goal is not simply a prettier website. It is a modern storefront that works on every device and helps customers find the right product faster — which improves conversion and makes far better use of the Shopify Plus platform you are already paying for.

3

Theme recommendation — Horizon

Your second question: “I still need to select a theme for my site. Should have that done in a couple of days.”

We recommend Horizon, Shopify’s own free theme.

  • Cost: $0. No licence fee, no renewal.
  • It covers everything this project needs. We checked the requirements against Horizon’s feature set — the mega menu from Section 1 and the sections, filtering, product-page layouts and mobile behaviour from Section 2 are all achievable on it.
  • First-party support. Being a Shopify theme, it tracks platform updates directly, which matters on Plus.
Worth being direct about: a paid theme would not buy you a better outcome here. On this site the gap is design and structure, not theme features. Spending on a premium theme and keeping the current layout would change very little; investing the same money into the redesign changes a great deal. Horizon plus the redesign in Section 4 is the better use of budget.
4

Proposed scope

4.1 Design phase — 20h

Full design for the three main page types, desktop and mobile:

  • Homepage — new section flow, hierarchy and spacing; brand colour direction applied across the page.
  • Collection page — category sidebar, restyled filters, product grid, pagination.
  • Product page — gallery, buy box, trust/support block, add-ons and related products.

Remaining pages (search, cart, account, content pages) are adapted to the same design system rather than individually designed — this is what keeps the estimate at 90h rather than several hundred.

4.2 Development phase — 70h

Includes everything in the design phase, built on Horizon, responsive on desktop and mobile, plus:

  • Mega menu — full-width, three-level, desktop and mobile (the 12h from Section 1 is included here, not charged twice).
  • Left-hand category navigation on collection pages — behaviour: it displays the sub-menu for the current category.
  • Collection filtering — the new technical filters (price, brand, size, grit, VOC, mix ratio and similar), with long filter groups truncated behind a Show more toggle.
  • Pagination replacing infinite load-more.
  • Product card Add to cart / Quick view, product-page add-ons, footer rebuild.
  • QA across browsers and breakpoints.

4.3 Apps — live chat, reviews, wishlist

The current site uses apps for live chat, reviews and wishlist. Our position:

  • We will recommend specific apps and discuss them with you once the design is agreed — app choice is best made against a settled design, not before it.
  • No additional setup fee. We advise on the apps and install them for you as part of this engagement.
  • Detailed configuration — the business rules inside each app — is handled by your team, and we will walk you through it.
  • If you would prefer us to do that detailed configuration, send us the specific requirements and we will quote it separately.

App subscription fees (if you choose a paid tier) are billed by the app vendors and are not included in the figures below.
